name: When Not to Use Blockchain
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Case for Boring Technology
lesson.summary: A practical decision framework for recognizing when a blockchain adds cost and complexity without adding real trust benefits, built on the limitations and alternatives covered so far.
lesson.body:
Combine Blockchain Limitations (slow throughput, growing storage, energy costs for proof of work, and immutability that cuts both ways) with the alternatives from the last chapter, and a practical question emerges: does this specific system actually need a blockchain, or would something simpler do the same job? Researchers have proposed decision frameworks along exactly these lines, walking through a short sequence of questions. Do you need to store shared state at all. Are there multiple parties who need to write to it. Is there already a trusted third party everyone would accept as an arbiter. Do the writers trust each other enough to just agree on a shared database.

A concrete example makes this vivid. Suppose a company wants to track its own warehouse inventory across several facilities. Every server that would participate is one the company itself operates. There is no adversarial party who might secretly rewrite history, because there is only one party. A centralized database with backups, access logs, and role-based permissions achieves the same tamper evidence goals as a blockchain here, at a fraction of the cost and with no consensus latency. Adding a blockchain to this design does not add security, it adds overhead that nobody needed.

Another strong signal is the need to fix mistakes. If a system must be able to correct a coding error, comply with a court order, or delete illegal or sensitive content, immutability is a liability rather than a feature. This becomes very concrete later in this chapter batch, in the Right to Be Forgotten chapter, where a real privacy law requires deletion capability that public blockchains structurally resist.

Privacy requirements point the same direction. If business confidentiality or a data protection law means not everyone should be able to see the data, a public blockchain is the wrong default design, a theme the next chapter develops in full. And if participants already trust a regulator, a bank, or a platform to arbitrate their disagreements, that trusted party can simply run an ordinary database. There is no need to engineer that party out of the picture by force through decentralization if nobody actually objects to their presence.

None of this means blockchain is a bad technology. It means its value proposition is trust minimization among parties who do not already trust each other and will not accept a central arbiter. Where that specific condition does not hold, boring technology, a database, a PKI certificate, a set of digitally signed documents, wins on cost, speed, simplicity, and the ability to fix errors when they inevitably happen.
